reference.source: Standard solid-organ transplantation and transplant immunology reference texts
clinicalPearls: Immune-mediated injury to a transplanted organ occurring over days to months, classically within the first few months but possible at any time, especially with inadequate immunosuppression or non-adherence
Two principal mechanisms operate: T-cell-mediated cellular rejection driven by recipient T lymphocytes, and antibody-mediated rejection driven by donor-specific antibodies against HLA
It is often clinically silent early and is detected as a rise in organ-specific markers, such as creatinine in the kidney or transaminases in the liver, or on protocol biopsy
Diagnosis rests on allograft biopsy with histological grading, supported by detection of donor-specific antibodies and complement split product C4d staining in antibody-mediated disease
Cell-mediated rejection shows mononuclear inflammatory infiltrates, whereas antibody-mediated rejection shows microvascular injury with C4d deposition
Risk factors include HLA mismatch, pre-existing sensitisation, previous transplants, and reduced or missed immunosuppression
First-line treatment of cellular rejection is high-dose corticosteroids, with lymphocyte-depleting or antibody therapy reserved for severe or steroid-resistant episodes
Antibody-mediated rejection is treated by removing or neutralising antibody, for example with plasma exchange and adjunctive agents, alongside optimised immunosuppression
reference.pathophysiology: Recipient immune cells recognise donor HLA through direct and indirect pathways of allorecognition. In cellular rejection, activated T lymphocytes infiltrate the graft and injure tubular, parenchymal, or endothelial targets. In antibody-mediated rejection, B cells and plasma cells produce donor-specific antibodies that bind graft microvascular endothelium, activate complement with deposition of the split product C4d, and cause microvascular inflammation and injury. Both processes compromise graft perfusion and function and, if unchecked, predispose to chronic rejection.
additionalDifferentials: Infection of the allograft such as BK nephropathy or cytomegalovirus disease
Recurrence of the primary disease within the graft
Surgical or vascular complications such as thrombosis, stenosis, or obstruction
Ischaemia-reperfusion injury or delayed graft function early after transplantation
Dehydration or outflow obstruction causing functional decline
additionalInvestigations: Allograft biopsy with histological grading, which is the diagnostic standard
Donor-specific antibody testing through HLA antibody screening
C4d immunostaining on biopsy for antibody-mediated rejection
Organ-specific function tests with trend monitoring
Immunosuppressant drug levels and assessment of adherence
Doppler ultrasound or other imaging to exclude vascular or mechanical causes
Screening for graft infection such as BK virus or cytomegalovirus where relevant
redFlags: Severe antibody-mediated rejection with widespread microvascular injury
Rejection from non-adherence or sensitisation with high donor-specific antibody levels
reference.prognosis: Many cellular rejection episodes reverse with prompt treatment, whereas antibody-mediated and steroid-resistant rejection carry a higher risk of graft loss and predispose to chronic rejection; early detection and treatment improve graft survival.
pitfalls: Attributing graft dysfunction to rejection without biopsy and missing infection or drug toxicity
Overlooking antibody-mediated rejection by not testing for donor-specific antibodies or C4d
Missing non-adherence as a cause, particularly in adolescents
Over-immunosuppressing and precipitating infection or malignancy
Failing to monitor for chronic rejection after an acute episode
references: Consensus histological classification of allograft rejection
management: Treat T-cell-mediated cellular rejection with pulsed high-dose corticosteroids, escalating steroid-resistant episodes to lymphocyte-depleting antithymocyte globulin

Manage antibody-mediated rejection by removing donor-specific antibody with plasma exchange and intravenous immunoglobulin, adding B-cell-directed rituximab or complement- or proteasome-targeted agents in refractory cases
Optimise maintenance immunosuppression with a calcineurin inhibitor, an antiproliferative agent and corticosteroid, and actively address non-adherence
Confirm the diagnosis and grade severity with allograft biopsy, supported by donor-specific antibody testing and C4d staining, before committing to treatment
Add infection prophylaxis against Pneumocystis, cytomegalovirus and fungi during periods of augmented immunosuppression
Monitor organ-specific function trends and donor-specific antibody levels to detect and track rejection
Manage within a specialist transplant multidisciplinary team with structured adherence and drug-level support
